title: Locomotion and Movement
description: Grade 11 Biology: types of movement and muscle, the structure and contraction of skeletal muscle, the human skeleton and joints, and disorders of the muscular and skeletal systems.

topics.title: Types of Movement and Muscle
topics.concept:
The ability to move is one of the signs of life. Movement is any change in the position of a body part, while locomotion is movement of the whole body from one place to another (like walking or swimming). All locomotion is movement, but not all movement is locomotion.

Human movements are of three main kinds: amoeboid (like some white blood cells moving with pseudopodia), ciliary (the beating of cilia, e.g. in the windpipe and oviducts), and muscular (movement of limbs, jaws, tongue, etc.) — the most important for locomotion. Muscular movement needs the coordinated action of muscles, bones and joints.

There are three types of muscle in the body:

  • Skeletal (striped/voluntary) muscle — attached to bones; it moves the body and is under our conscious control. It appears striped (striated) under the microscope.
  • Smooth (unstriped/involuntary) muscle — found in the walls of internal organs like the stomach, intestines and blood vessels; it works automatically, not under our control.
  • Cardiac muscle — found only in the heart; it is striped but works involuntarily and never tires.

Muscles have special properties: they can contract (shorten), are extensible (can be stretched), elastic (return to shape) and excitable (respond to a stimulus).

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the difference between movement and locomotion?
examples.solution:
Compare a part vs the whole body.

  • Movement is any change in position of a body part.
  • Locomotion is movement of the whole body from one place to another.
examples.answer: Movement is any change in position of a part; locomotion is movement of the whole body from place to place.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the three types of muscle and say which is under conscious control.
examples.solution:
List the muscle types.

  • Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.
  • Skeletal (voluntary) muscle is under conscious control.
examples.answer: Skeletal, smooth and cardiac; skeletal (voluntary) muscle is under conscious control.

examples.problem: Example 3: Where is cardiac muscle found, and what is special about it?
examples.solution:
It is in one organ.

  • Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.
  • It is striped but involuntary and never tires.
examples.answer: Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart; it is striped, involuntary and never tires.

recap:
• Movement = change in position of a part; locomotion = whole-body movement.
  • Types: amoeboid, ciliary, muscular (main for locomotion).
  • Three muscles: skeletal (striped, voluntary, on bones), smooth (unstriped, involuntary, organs), cardiac (heart, striped, involuntary, tireless).
  • Muscle properties: contractile, extensible, elastic, excitable.

quiz.q: Movement of the whole body from one place to another is:
quiz.explanation: Locomotion is whole-body movement from place to place.

quiz.q: The muscle found only in the heart is:
quiz.explanation: Cardiac muscle occurs only in the heart and is involuntary.

topics.title: Skeletal Muscle and Its Contraction
topics.concept:
Skeletal muscles move the body by pulling on bones. A muscle is made of bundles of long muscle fibres; each fibre contains many thread-like myofibrils. The myofibrils are made of two kinds of protein filaments: thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin. The regular, overlapping arrangement of these gives skeletal muscle its striped (striated) look. The repeating unit between two lines (Z-lines) is called a sarcomere — the functional unit of contraction.

How does a muscle contract? According to the sliding filament theory, the thin actin filaments slide over the thick myosin filaments, so the sarcomere shortens — the filaments themselves do not shrink, they just slide past each other. This needs a nerve signal, calcium ions and energy from ATP. When the muscle relaxes, the filaments slide back. Many sarcomeres shortening together make the whole muscle contract and pull the bone.

Muscles can only pull, not push, so they work in pairs called antagonistic muscles. For example, at the elbow the biceps contracts to bend (flex) the arm while the triceps relaxes; to straighten the arm, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. The muscle that bends a joint is a flexor; the one that straightens it is an extensor. This teamwork lets us make precise, controlled movements.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the two protein filaments responsible for muscle contraction.
examples.solution:
One thick, one thin.

  • Thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin.

examples.problem: Example 2: State the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction.
examples.solution:
Filaments slide, not shrink.

  • The thin actin filaments slide over the thick myosin filaments.
  • This shortens the sarcomere and contracts the muscle (needs Ca²⁺ and ATP).
examples.answer: Contraction happens when actin filaments slide over myosin filaments, shortening the sarcomere (using calcium and ATP).

examples.problem: Example 3: How do the biceps and triceps work together at the elbow?
examples.solution:
They are antagonistic muscles.

  • To bend the arm, the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes.
  • To straighten it, the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes.
examples.answer: They are antagonistic: biceps contracts (triceps relaxes) to bend the arm; triceps contracts (biceps relaxes) to straighten it.

recap:
• Skeletal muscle: fibres → myofibrils → actin (thin) + myosin (thick) filaments; unit = sarcomere.
  • Sliding filament theory: actin slides over myosin → sarcomere shortens (needs Ca²⁺ + ATP).
  • Muscles only pull → work in antagonistic pairs (biceps/triceps; flexor/extensor).

quiz.q: According to the sliding filament theory, during contraction the actin filaments:
quiz.explanation: Actin slides over myosin, shortening the sarcomere; filaments do not shrink.

quiz.q: Muscles that work in opposing pairs, like biceps and triceps, are:
quiz.explanation: Antagonistic muscles act in opposition to move a joint both ways.

topics.title: The Skeleton, Joints and Disorders
topics.concept:
The framework that supports the body and gives muscles something to pull on is the skeleton. The human skeleton has about 206 bones in an adult and is divided into two parts: the axial skeleton (the central axis — skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum) and the appendicular skeleton (the limbs and the girdles that attach them). The skeleton gives shape and support, protects delicate organs (the skull protects the brain, the ribs protect the heart and lungs), allows movement (with muscles), makes blood cells (in the bone marrow) and stores minerals like calcium.

The place where two or more bones meet is a joint. Joints are of different kinds:

  • Movable (synovial) joints — allow free movement. Examples: the ball-and-socket joint (shoulder, hip — movement in all directions) and the hinge joint (elbow, knee — movement in one plane, like a door).
  • Slightly movable joints — allow a little movement (e.g. between vertebrae).
  • Immovable (fixed) joints — allow no movement (e.g. the bones of the skull).

Bones are joined by tough cords called ligaments, and muscles are joined to bones by tendons. Common disorders of the muscular and skeletal system include arthritis (inflammation and pain in joints), osteoporosis (bones become weak and brittle, often in older people due to low calcium), muscular dystrophy (progressive weakening of muscles) and gout (joint inflammation from uric-acid crystals). A diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, plus regular exercise, keeps bones and muscles strong.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the two main divisions of the human skeleton.
examples.solution:
The skeleton has a central and a limb part.

  • The axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum).
  • The appendicular skeleton (limbs and girdles).
examples.answer: The axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton.

examples.problem: Example 2: Compare a ball-and-socket joint with a hinge joint, giving one example of each.
examples.solution:
They differ in range of movement.

  • Ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip): movement in all directions.
  • Hinge (elbow, knee): movement in one plane only.
examples.answer: A ball-and-socket joint (shoulder/hip) moves in all directions; a hinge joint (elbow/knee) moves in one plane only.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is osteoporosis, and how can it be prevented?
examples.solution:
It weakens bones.

  • Osteoporosis is the weakening of bones (brittle), often from low calcium in older age.
  • It is prevented by a calcium- and vitamin-D-rich diet and exercise.
examples.answer: Osteoporosis is the weakening/brittleness of bones; it is prevented by enough calcium and vitamin D and regular exercise.

recap:
• Skeleton (~206 bones): axial (skull, vertebrae, ribs, sternum) + appendicular (limbs, girdles); gives support, protection, movement, blood cells, mineral store.
  • Joints: movable/synovial (ball-and-socket, hinge), slightly movable, immovable (skull).
  • Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.
  • Disorders: arthritis, osteoporosis, muscular dystrophy, gout.

quiz.q: The shoulder and hip are examples of a:
quiz.explanation: The shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket joints, allowing all-round movement.

quiz.q: Weak, brittle bones, often due to low calcium in older age, is:
quiz.explanation: Osteoporosis is the weakening and brittleness of bones.

questions.q: Movement of the whole body from one place to another is:
questions.explanation: Locomotion is whole-body movement from place to place.

questions.q: The movement of cilia in the windpipe is an example of:
questions.explanation: Beating cilia produce ciliary movement.

questions.q: Muscle attached to bones and under conscious control is:
questions.explanation: Skeletal (voluntary) muscle moves bones under conscious control.

questions.q: Muscle found in the walls of internal organs is:
questions.explanation: Smooth (involuntary) muscle lines internal organs.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle is found in the:
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle occurs only in the heart.

questions.q: The thick filaments of a muscle are made of:
questions.explanation: Thick filaments are myosin; thin filaments are actin.

questions.q: The functional unit of muscle contraction is the:
questions.explanation: The sarcomere (between Z-lines) is the unit of contraction.

questions.q: In the sliding filament theory, the actin filaments:
questions.explanation: Actin slides over myosin to shorten the sarcomere.

questions.q: Muscle contraction needs calcium ions and energy from:
questions.explanation: Contraction requires Ca²⁺ and ATP energy.

questions.q: Biceps and triceps are an example of:
questions.explanation: They work as an antagonistic pair at the elbow.

questions.q: About how many bones are there in the adult human skeleton?
questions.explanation: The adult human skeleton has about 206 bones.

questions.q: The skull, vertebral column and ribs belong to the:
questions.explanation: These central bones form the axial skeleton.

questions.q: The elbow and knee are examples of a:
questions.explanation: Elbow and knee are hinge joints (one-plane movement).

questions.q: Bones are joined to other bones by tough cords called:
questions.explanation: Ligaments join bone to bone; tendons join muscle to bone.

questions.q: Inflammation and pain in the joints is called:
questions.explanation: Arthritis is inflammation and pain of the joints.

questions.q: Muscles are arranged in antagonistic pairs because a muscle can only:
questions.explanation: Since a muscle only pulls, an opposing muscle is needed to move the bone the other way.

questions.q: During contraction the sarcomere shortens even though the filaments stay the same length. This is explained by:
options: The filaments sliding past each other
questions.explanation: The sliding filament theory: overlap increases as filaments slide, shortening the sarcomere without changing filament length.

questions.q: A blow to the head is less likely to damage the brain because the skull is made of:
options: Immovable joints forming a protective case
questions.explanation: The fixed, immovable joints of the skull form a rigid protective box around the brain.

questions.q: Older people are more prone to fractures partly because of osteoporosis, in which bones:
questions.explanation: Loss of bone minerals like calcium makes bones weak and easy to break.

questions.q: The shoulder allows a wider range of movement than the elbow because it is a:
questions.explanation: A ball-and-socket joint permits movement in all directions, unlike the one-plane hinge elbow.

questions.q: Without enough ATP, a muscle cannot relax properly (as in cramps) because ATP is needed to:
options: Detach the filaments and reset the sarcomere
questions.explanation: ATP is required both for contraction and to release the cross-bridges so the muscle can relax.
